links.note: 851 defines இகல் as the disease (நோய்) that spreads பகல், the ill nature of division, among all living beings. 886 takes the same division to its end inside one's own circle: if ஒன்றாமை arises among ஒன்றியார், escaping death (பொன்றாமை) is hard at any time. The general diagnosis of 851 becomes a specific warning about a ruler's own people; Parimelazhagar reads 886 of a king.

851 names the fault as பகல், splitting apart, and its chapter closes (860) by setting நகல் against இகல். 187 uses the same pair of roots: those who do not know how to make friends by நகச்சொல்லி will பகச்சொல்லி and separate even their kin. The chapter on backbiting already holds the contrast between dividing and laughing together that the chapter on hostility is built on.

852 says that even if another, intending division, does what is unbearable (பற்றா செயினும்), not doing harm in return out of hostility is best (இன்னா செய்யாமை தலை). 312 says the same of the spotless: even when someone has done harm in rancour (கறுத்து இன்னா செய்த அக்கண்ணும்), not doing harm back (மறுத்து இன்னா செய்யாமை) is their settled stand. The rule given to renouncers in Book 1 is repeated in the Book of Wealth as advice on handling opponents.

852 ranks not harming a provoker as தலை, the best course. 203 uses the same ranking word: the head of all understanding (அறிவினுள் எல்லாம் தலை) is not to do evil even to those who hate you (செறுவார்க்கும்). Together they show the text treating non-retaliation as a matter of good sense as well as of virtue; Parimelazhagar on 852 explains that retaliating feeds the enmity while refraining lets it die out.

853 says that removing the painful disease of hostility gives a brightness that neither fails nor is flawed (தவலில்லாத் தாவில் விளக்கம்), which Parimelazhagar takes as lasting fame. 156 says those who punish have one day's pleasure while those who forbear have praise until the end (பொன்றுந் துணையும் புகழ்). Both make enduring renown the result of declining the quarrel, one in the householder's ethics and one in public life.

854 says that if hostility, 'the suffering of sufferings', is destroyed (இகலென்னும் துன்பத்துள் துன்பங் கெடின்), it yields the joy of joys. 369 has the same closing line with craving in place of hostility: அவாவென்னும் துன்பத்துள் துன்பங் கெடின், joy is unbroken even here. The same formula names அவா as the chief misery for the renouncer and இகல் as the chief misery in worldly dealings.

854 offers இன்பத்துள் இன்பம், the joy of joys, as what follows when hostility goes. 629 uses the same two phrases differently: one who does not crave pleasure within pleasure (இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் விழையாதான்) does not feel pain within pain (துன்பத்துள் துன்பம் உறுதல் இலன்). Read together, the joy 854 promises is a result of removing a cause of suffering, and 629 warns against making such joy an object of desire.

855 asks who would be inclined to overcome those able to lean away when hostility confronts them (இகலெதிர் சாய்ந்தொழுக வல்லாரை). 985 says the strength of the capable is to bow (பணிதல்), and that this is the weapon by which the worthy change their opponents (மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை). Both treat yielding as what disarms an opponent; 985 states it as a trait of the சான்றோர், 855 as a skill (வல்லார்), which Parimelazhagar says is hard for kings.

855 says no one sets out to defeat a person who can lean away from hostility. 874 goes a step further: the world rests in the greatness of the person of character who conducts himself taking enmity as friendship (பகை நட்பாக் கொண்டொழுகும்). 855 describes safety gained by not answering hostility; 874 describes actively turning the enemy into a friend and gives it a public value.

855 holds that the one who gives way before hostility cannot be beaten. In 1327 the man says that in a lovers' sulk the one who loses has won (ஊடலில் தோற்றவர் வென்றார்), as the reunion shows. The speaker in 1327 is a lover talking about play-quarrels, so this is the same pattern of winning by yielding in a different setting, not a doctrine shared with 855.

856 says the life of one who declares it sweet to excel in hostility (இகலின் மிகல் இனிது என்பவன்) is close to failure and ruin. 307 says the ruin of one who takes anger to be a thing of worth (சினத்தைப் பொருளென்று கொண்டவன்) is as sure as the hand of one who strikes the ground. In both the fault is the valuing of the passion, and both attach certain or imminent ruin to it.

856 warns the person who finds prevailing in hostility sweet (இனிது) that failure and ruin are near (நணித்து). 156 measures that sweetness: those who punish get one day's pleasure (ஒருநாளை இன்பம்), and those who bear get praise to the end. 156 grants the pleasure and limits it to a day; 856 adds what follows it.

423 defines understanding as seeing the true thing (மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்பது அறிவு) in whatever one hears from anyone. 857 says those of harmful understanding who are attached to hostility (இகல்மேவல் இன்னா அறிவினவர்) do not see the மெய்ப்பொருள் that carries victory. So 857 names hostility as one thing that turns அறிவு against its defining task; Parimelazhagar narrows மெய்ப்பொருள் here to the content of the treatises on statecraft and says hostility clouds the understanding.

no_link_reason: Its gain/ruin antithesis is the chapter's own refrain (855, 859); the closest outside parallel, 180, is proposed under 860 where the wording matches more closely.

links.note: 859 says that when gain is coming a person does not look at hostility (இகல் காணான்), and when he is to bring ruin on himself he looks to excel in it. 372 says a fate of loss makes a person foolish and a fate of gain enlarges understanding. 859 does not name fate, but it has the same order of events, the turn of mind preceding the turn of fortune, and Manakkudavar reads it that way, saying hostility does not arise in those with good deeds behind them.

860 says all ills come from hostility, and from friendly gladness (நகல்) comes 'the pride called good conduct' (நன்னயம் என்னும் செருக்கு). 180 has the same shape and the same closing phrase: coveting without thought yields destruction, and 'the pride called not-wanting' (வேண்டாமை என்னும் செருக்கு) yields victory. In both the verse sets a ruinous impulse against its absence and calls that absence a செருக்கு, which Parimelazhagar glosses in both places as wealth.

860 says இகலான் ஆம் இன்னாத எல்லாம்: every painful thing arises from hostility. 303 says to forget anger toward anyone, because the birth of evils comes from it (தீய பிறத்தல் அதனான் வரும்). The Book of Virtue makes anger the source of evils and the Book of Wealth makes hostility the source, with nearly the same construction.

860 credits நகல், glad friendliness, with producing good conduct and its dignity. 999 describes those without the capacity: for people not able to laugh with others (நகல் வல்லர் அல்லார்) the wide world lies in darkness even by day. 860 gives what நகல் yields and 999 what its absence costs; Parimelazhagar reads நகல் in both as rejoicing in company with others.

861 advises avoiding opposition to the stronger (வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக) and embracing enmity toward the weaker (மெலியார்மேல் மேக பகை). 250 uses the same pair of words to the opposite effect: when going against those weaker than yourself (மெலியார்மேல் செல்லுமிடத்து), think of yourself before the stronger (வலியார்முன்). The conflict holds if 861 is read as general advice; on Parimelazhagar's reading 861 is a king's calculation and 250 speaks to the person without அருள், so they address different agents. Kalaignar avoids the conflict by reading 861 in the reverse sense.

861 ends with a positive command to favour enmity against the weak (மேக பகை). 871, ten verses later, says the thing called enmity, which has no good in it (பண்பிலதனை), is not to be wanted even in jest. The two conflict if 871 is read without exception; Parimelazhagar limits 871 to enmity that is not advantageous, which leaves room for 861.

471 tells one to weigh the strength of the task, one's own strength, the opponent's strength (மாற்றான் வலி) and the allies' strength before acting. 861 gives the decision rule that follows from the weighing: decline the contest with the stronger, accept it with the weaker. Parimelazhagar connects them, saying 'strong' and 'weak' in 861 include the strength of allies.

862 asks how a man with no love, no worthy allies (ஆன்ற துணையிலன்) and no strength of his own can wear down an enemy's might. 449 states the principle: those without capital have no profit, and those without the prop of supporters (மதலையாஞ் சார்பிலார்) have no standing. 862 applies to a contest with an enemy what 449 says of a ruler's position in general.

862 describes the man without love, allies or strength as unable to resist an enemy. 873 judges the man in that position who nevertheless provokes: one who, alone (தமியனாய்), takes on the enmity of many is more foolish than the mad. 862 gives the weak position seen by an attacker; 873 gives the advice that follows for the one who is in it.

382 lists four things that must never fail in a king: fearlessness, giving, understanding and drive (அஞ்சாமை ஈகை அறிவு ஊக்கம்). 863 lists the man who is very easy for an enemy: he fears, does not know, does not fit with others, does not give (அஞ்சும் அறியான் அமைவிலன் ஈகலான்). Three of the four items are the kingly qualities negated, so the easy target of 863 is the failed king of 382.

863 puts fear first among the traits that make a man easy for his enemy. 534 says the fearful have no fortress (அச்சமுடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை); Parimelazhagar explains that defences are of no use to one with fear in his mind. Both say that fear cancels whatever other protection a person has.

863 lists fear and ignorance among the weaknesses that make a man easy prey (அஞ்சும் அறியான்). 869 keeps just those two and states them from the other side: joy does not go far from those who fight if they get enemies who are without understanding and afraid (அறிவிலா அஞ்சும் பகைவர்ப் பெறின்). The chapter moves from describing the weak enemy to stating what the attacker gains from him.

864 says one who does not leave off anger (நீங்கான் வெகுளி) and has no நிறை is easy for anyone, at any time, anywhere. 305 says that if you would guard yourself, guard against anger, because unguarded anger kills oneself (தன்னையே கொல்லுஞ் சினம்). 305 states the self-destruction as an ethical fact; 864 shows how it works in a contest, by making the angry man open to any opponent.

864 says the man who cannot leave anger is easy for anyone to overcome. 526 gives the opposite case: no one on earth has more people at his side than one who gives greatly and does not cherish anger (பேணான் வெகுளி). Put together, anger decides whether a man stands with many around him or exposed to all.

865 lists a man who does not look to the path (வழி நோக்கான்), does not do what is fitting, does not look to blame (பழி நோக்கான்) and has no character, and calls him a pleasure to his foes. 833 defines the fool by a similar list of absences: no shame, no inquiry, no affection, no care for anything (நாணாமை நாடாமை நாரின்மை யாதொன்றும் பேணாமை). The same portrait is drawn once as a moral type and once as a strategic opportunity for an enemy.

866 says the enmity of a man of blind anger and excessive lust (காணாச் சினத்தான் கழிபெருங் காமத்தான்) is to be welcomed. 360 names the same two, with delusion, as what must perish for suffering to perish (காமம் வெகுளி மயக்கம்). What the chapter on true knowledge treats as obstacles to release, the chapter on enemies treats as what makes an opponent beatable; Parimelazhagar says such men destroy themselves.

867 says the enmity of one who stays close and does unfitting things must be obtained even at a price: கொடுத்தும் கொளல்வேண்டும் ... பகை. 794 uses the identical phrase for the opposite relation: the friendship of a well-born person who is ashamed of blame கொடுத்தும் கொளல்வேண்டும் நட்பு. The repeated wording treats enmity, like friendship, as something chosen and worth paying for when the person is right for it.

867 advises paying to have a certain man as an enemy rather than keep him near. 800 advises paying to be rid of a certain friend: give something (ஒன்று ஈத்தும்) and leave the friendship of those who are not a match. Both accept a cost to end a harmful closeness; the commentators differ on who the man in 867 is, Parimelazhagar taking him as one who begins a task and acts unsuitably, Kalaignar as one who stays beside you.

504 tells the ruler to examine a man's qualities, then his faults, and judge by what predominates (மிகை நாடி மிக்க கொளல்). 868 describes the result when the tally is all on one side: with no qualities and many faults (குணனிலனாய்க் குற்றம் பலவாயின்) he is left without companions, and that is a support to his opponents. The test used for choosing servants in 504 is applied by 868 to the ruler himself, with his enemies as the ones who benefit.

868 says a man without qualities and with many faults comes to have no one with him (இனனிலனாம்). 525 gives the positive case: one who can give and speak pleasantly will be surrounded by kin in rows (அடுக்கிய சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்படும்). Both make a person's following a product of his character; 868 adds the military consequence of losing it.

869 says joy does not go far from those who fight if they get enemies who are ignorant and afraid. 772 says holding the spear that missed an elephant is sweeter (இனிது) than holding the arrow that hit a forest hare. One locates the pleasure of fighting in the easy opponent and the other in the hard one; the conflict holds if both are read as claims about what a fighter should want, and eases if 869 is a king's reckoning of advantage and 772 an individual warrior's sense of honour.

no_link_reason: The syntax is disputed and the three commentators give three different senses (Parimelazhagar: fame avoids one who will not take the easy gain of fighting the unlearned; Manakkudavar: fame never comes to an enemy who is unlearned, angry and of small means; Kalaignar differs again), so no link is built on it.
